en: The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Girl Yaya.
Translator unknown; appended to the Catalogue of the Western Jin.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time...

At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada took a wife for his son, obtaining the daughter of a wealthy and noble householder. She was peerlessly beautiful, yet she was arrogant and haughty; she did not attend to her mother-in-law, father-in-law, or husband with the proper etiquette of a wife.
The Anāthapiṇḍada family deliberated among themselves, saying:
"His wife is arrogant; by what means should she be instructed?
If we were to strike her with a staff, it would not be a wholesome method."
"If there is no instruction, their transgressions will increase day by day. Elder!
Only the Buddha, the Great Sage, is well able to provide such instruction. Prepare offerings and arrange a vegetarian feast; invite the Buddha for tomorrow."

The Buddha accepted the invitation. On the following day, the Buddha arrived leading his assembly of disciples. All the members of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada’s family came out to pay their respects to the Buddha, but Yuyē did not come out.

The Buddha immediately emitted a great radiance of purple-gold color that illuminated the interior of Yuyē’s chamber. The Buddha manifested the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics; when Yuyē beheld the Buddha’s radiant appearance, she was struck with great alarm and fear. Feeling a sense of dread, she then went out to pay her respects to the Buddha.
The Buddha told Yuye:

"It is not the way of women to give rise to arrogance based on physical beauty. Having a handsome appearance is not true beauty; only upright conduct of the mind is true beauty, for it is that which is loved and respected by others. One must not rely on a beautiful countenance to be arrogant and self-indulgent, lest one be reborn in a lowly station as a servant to others."
The Buddha said to Yuye:
"Is it not the case that the nature of women involves three obstructions and ten evils, yet they do not realize this themselves?
Yuye addressed the Buddha:
“What are the three obstructions and the ten evils?
The Buddha told Yuye:

“First, the obstruction by one’s parents during childhood; second, the obstruction by one’s husband after marriage; third, the obstruction by one’s children in old age. These are the three obstructions.”
What are the ten evils?
First, at the time of birth, one's parents do not rejoice.
Second, there is no joy in raising and nurturing [the child].
Third, they are constantly anxious about marriage and the failure to observe proper rites.
Fourth, they fear people everywhere.
Fifth, they are separated from their parents.
Sixth, relying on the doors of others;
seventh, great difficulty in becoming pregnant;
eighth, difficulty at the time of childbirth.
"Ninth, she is constantly fearful of her husband.
Tenth, she never attains autonomy. These are the ten evils.
When Suyā heard the Buddha speak of the three obstructions and the ten evils, her body and mind trembled with dread, and she addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will teach me the laws for being a wife.
The Buddha told Yuye:
“The laws for being a wife should consist of five grades.”
What are the five? First, like a mother’s wife;
second, like a minister’s wife; third, like a sister’s wife; fourth, a maidservant’s wife; and fifth, one’s own wife.
What is meant by a "mother-wife"?
Because she loves her husband as if he were her son, she is called a mother-wife.
What is meant by a "subject-wife"?
Because she serves her husband as she would a sovereign, she is called a "minister-wife.
What is meant by a "younger-sister wife"?
Because she serves her husband as she would an elder brother, she is called a "younger-sister wife."
What is meant by a "slave-wife"?
Because she serves her husband like a concubine, she is called a slave-wife.
What is meant by a "husband-and-wife" [relationship]?

To turn one's back on kin and incline toward strangers is to forever depart from those who gave birth; though bound by affection and intimacy, sharing a common heart yet possessing different forms, one should honor and serve with reverence and caution, free from prideful arrogance. To skillfully attend to both internal and external family members so that the household is abundant and prosperous, and to receive guests with hospitality while extolling their good reputations—this is the way of husband and wife.
The Buddha told Yuye:
"Serving one's mother-in-law, father-in-law, and husband also involves five virtues and three evils.
Yuye addressed the Buddha:
“What are the five virtues and three evils?
The Buddha told Yuye:

“The first is to sleep late and rise early to manage the household affairs; whatever fine food there may be, do not put it to your own mouth, but first offer it to your mother-in-law, father-in-law, and husband.”
Second, look after the household goods so that nothing is lost or neglected.
Third, guard your speech, practice patience, and remain free from anger.
Fourth, maintain a dignified and solemn demeanor, exercising caution and constant vigilance, always fearing that you may fall short.

Fifth, with a single mind, she serves her mother-in-law, father-in-law, and husband with reverence and filial piety, thereby establishing a good reputation, bringing joy to her kin, and being praised by others; these are the five virtues.
What are the three evils?
First, she goes to bed early before nightfall and does not rise when the sun comes up; when her husband rebukes her with anger, she instead responds with resentment and insults.
Second, she eats fine food herself while giving poor food to her mother-in-law, father-in-law, and husband; she is licentious, deceitful, and employs ten thousand forms of sorcery and wickedness.

Third is not to be mindful of one's livelihood while wandering through the world, speaking of others' strengths and weaknesses, seeking out their faults, engaging in quarrels and idle chatter, causing resentment and jealousy among kinsmen, and being despised by others; these are the three evils.
Upon hearing the Buddha’s discourse on the five virtues and three evils, Yuyé felt faith, reverence, and joy, and was moved by a sense of shame and remorse.

She addressed the Buddha, saying: “I, your disciple, have been foolish. Before I had seen the Buddha and before I had heard the Dharma, I committed immeasurable faults and obstacles without realizing them myself.

Now that I have heard this teaching, my mind has been awakened and enlightened; I realize that all my past actions were wrong. From this day forward, I shall reform my past ways and cultivate my future conduct in accordance with what the Honored One has taught, never again daring to transgress.”

"I only pray that the Holy World-Honored One, out of compassion and mercy, will grant me relief, hear my confession so that my transgressions may be cleared away, and accept my five precepts so that I may become a disciple.
The Buddha said, "Excellent!"
"Yuye! I accept your repentance;
do not commit such acts again. I grant you the precepts; receive them with reverence and practice them.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
"Listen attentively and reflect upon this well.
Yuye replied, "So be it,
World-Honored One!"
"I vow to joyfully receive and uphold it.
The Buddha told Yuye:
"As for upholding one precept: with one's own hands and body, one shall not kill, extending this kindness to all living beings."
Those who uphold the two precepts are pure, benevolent, and yielding, refraining from theft; they diminish their own needs to aid the multitude.
Those who uphold the three precepts are chaste and refrain from sexual misconduct, ensuring their conduct remains untainted.
Those who uphold the four precepts must not speak falsely, even in jest.
Those who uphold the five precepts distance themselves from alcohol, neither drinking it nor committing various evils.
They protect and maintain these prohibitive precepts as if their heads were on fire.
Observe for yourself that this physical form cannot endure long; life is as precarious as a flash of lightning and passes by like a breeze through a courtyard.
Youth must inevitably decay, so do not rely upon your beauty; you should instead diligently apply yourself with vigor and renounce worldly glory, in accordance with the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas.
If you now practice cultivation, you shall attain Buddhahood; the Way of the Buddha must be studied, and the sutras must be heard.

Now that I have attained Buddhahood, I proclaim this Mahayana teaching brought about by my own excellence: there is neither man nor woman; whoever delights in hearing the Dharma shall obtain what they wish according to their aspirations.
Yujia addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
What kind of prosperity shall a virtuous wife obtain?"
"What fault shall that evil wife incur?
The Buddha told Yuye:

"The virtuous wife receives honor and renown in her present life; her kinfolk hold her in high esteem. She receives blessings and is reborn in the heavens. When her lifespan in heaven ends, she returns to the human world, where she is respected by all among the descendants of kings and nobles, wherever she may be born."

As for that wicked wife, everyone detests and envies her, finding no way to endure her; they wish for her to die soon. When her life ends, she shall fall into the realms of hell, animals, or servitude, transmigrating through them without any prospect of escape.

Upon hearing this discourse on the laws of virtuous and unvirtuous wives, Yuyaya was filled with awe and trepidation. She practiced with sincere devotion and immediately attained the fruit of the Path. She fashioned carvings and embroideries, created jeweled curtains, hung silken banners and canopies, and burned various famous incenses. As she circumambulated the stupa chanting hymns, her voice reached the ten directions; those who saw her rejoiced and prostrated before the shrine hall.
Ānanda said to the Buddha,
"What should this sutra be named?
The Buddha replied:
"This sutra is titled 'The Instruction of Women' and is also called the *Yujie jing*.
If women hear this sutra, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, and practice according to the Dharma, they shall cast off this female body and never again undergo rebirth as such."
When this sutra was being spoken, the great assembly rejoiced, prostrated, and practiced accordingly.
The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Girl Yaya.
